chunks: Handling and disposing of LiPos. The question: Why is it important to properly handle and dispose LiPos?
A LiPo packs a lot of energy into a soft, thin pouch with a flammable liquid inside.
Handling it carelessly can short it out or damage it internally, and the damage is not always visible.
Safe handling means protecting the terminals and the pouch, storing it half-charged and charging it carefully.
Safe disposal means taking it to battery recycling, never the regular trash.
Picture a loaded mousetrap in a thin paper bag. It is harmless while it sits still. Toss it in a pocket with your keys and something may set it off.
A crushed or punctured pack is similar: the harm can come right away or later. A pack that looks fine after a drop may still be damaged inside.
The dangerous region is any low-resistance contact: wire, tool, coin.

The contact dissipates a maximum of V squared over (4R int) equals 88 watts when its resistance matches the cell's, and the cell itself heats even more at the lowest contact resistances (the red curve runs off the top of the chart, to about 340 watts at 1 milliohms).
Together that is hundreds of watts split between a small cell and a few grams of metal.
Short circuit: an unintended low-resistance path across the terminals that lets huge current flow ("Short-circuiting a LiPo"). Storage voltage: about 3.
8 volts per cell, roughly half full ("LiPo storage charge"). Swelling: a puffed pouch caused by gas, a sign of damage to retire.
Take-back point: a collection spot or recycler that accepts lithium batteries safely.
Balance lead: the extra connector on a multi-cell pack ("Balance charging and when it is needed").
A loose 2 Ah cell with 50 milliohms internal resistance is dropped in a pocket, and a key touches both terminals with a 20 milliohms contact. The current is 4. 2 over (0.
05 plus 0. 02) equals 60 amps. The contact point heats at about 60 squared times 0. 02 equals 72 watts, which is why this can start a fire.
Putting caps or tape over the terminals avoids it. At end of life, tape the terminals and take the pack to a battery drop-off. That is the whole idea.
"LiPos are soft pouch cells holding a lot of energy and a flammable electrolyte, so puncture, crush, heat or shorted terminals can start an internal short and thermal runaway, even hours later.
So I store them insulated, at a partial charge, cool, in a fire-safe bag, charge them only with the right charger and never unattended, and retire swollen ones.
At end of life they go to battery recycling, with the terminals taped and the pack discharged, never in household trash where compactors crush them and start fires."
